title: Singly exponential shortest solutions of word equations
formal:
Do positive integers \(c,k\) exist such that every satisfiable word equation \(u=v\), over every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of constant letters and a disjoint finite set \(\mathcal X\) of variables, has a solution \(h\) satisfying
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|\le 2^{c(n+1)^k},\qquad n=|u|+|v|?\]
Here \(\mathcal X\) consists exactly of the variables occurring in the equation, each occurrence contributes one to \(n\), and the maximum over no variables is zero. A solution replaces each variable consistently by a finite word over \(\Sigma\), possibly empty, fixes the constant letters and makes the two expanded words identical.

The same constants \(c,k\) must work independently of the equation, the alphabet and the number of variables. This is the polynomial-exponent meaning of singly exponential. A linear exponent is welcome but is not required.
why: Very short equations can describe solutions whose expanded words are enormous. A universal singly exponential shortest-solution bound would constrain this hidden growth and, by the source’s compression theorem, imply NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability. This links a basic combinatorial question about strings to the unresolved complexity of exact string constraints.

progress.text: ICALP 1998 presents Conjecture B and the theorem showing that its affirmative answer implies NP membership of word-equation satisfiability.
The third arXiv version of Jeż’s paper includes an independent derivation of the doubly exponential shortest-solution bound.
STACS publishes the three-variable structural improvement while retaining the general NP-membership question.

definitions:
For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) consists of all finite sequences of its letters, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Multiplication is concatenation, and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity. The length \(|w|\) is the number of letters in the sequence \(w\), with \(|\varepsilon|=0\). Distinct constant letters are distinct symbols, not variables or numbers. The alphabet may have any finite cardinality; if it is empty, its only word is \(\varepsilon\).

An equation is a pair of explicitly written words \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Each variable and each constant occurrence counts as one symbol in the equation size \(n\). No compressed input, binary-encoded repeat operator, regular-language membership condition, length constraint, inequality, involution or cancellation operation is supplied. Exponent notation in an example of an equation is only shorthand for its fully expanded string, and its expanded length is charged. Variables may occur arbitrarily many times and may appear on either or both sides.

A solution is a monoid morphism \(h:(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\to\Sigma^*\) that fixes every \(a\in\Sigma\) and satisfies \(h(u)=h(v)\). Equivalently, choose one word \(h(x)\in\Sigma^*\) for each variable, substitute the same word at every occurrence, and concatenate in the original order. Empty substitutions are allowed, and no letter outside \(\Sigma\) may occur in a substitution. This is solving an equation in a free monoid, not in a free group or a semigroup with mandatory nonempty substitutions.

For a satisfiable equation, define
\[m(u,v)=\min_{h:\,h(u)=h(v)}\ \max_{x\in\mathcal X}|h(x)|.\]
The minimum exists because the feasible lengths form a nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers. The claim is \(m(u,v)\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\) for all satisfiable equations. It asks for at least one bounded solution to each equation, not for a bound on every solution. An equation can have infinitely many solutions with unbounded lengths and still satisfy the proposed shortest-solution bound.

The source also measures a solution by the length of the common expanded word \(h(u)=h(v)\). For each solution with \(M=\max_x|h(x)|\), every occurring variable image is a factor of that common word, and
\[M\le |h(u)|\le n\max(1,M).\]
These inequalities also cover the no-variable case using \(M=0\). Thus existence of a singly exponential bound on the shortest common-word length and the displayed variable-image bound are equivalent after changing the universal polynomial in the exponent. The card does not assert equality of these two minimum-length quantities.

The negative answer is the quantified assertion that for every pair of positive integers \(c,k\), some satisfiable equation has no solution meeting \(\max_x|h(x)|\le2^{c(n+1)^k}\). It is not enough to exhibit an exponential-length solution when a shorter one exists, or to beat one chosen polynomial exponent. No efficient construction of a solution or of a counterexample family is part of this nonconstructive length question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the universal singly exponential bound. A proof must provide fixed positive integers \(c,k\) and prove the bound for all satisfiable equations under the free-monoid and explicit-symbol conventions. A refutation must prove that every such polynomial-exponent bound fails. Bounds for a fixed number of variables, bounded occurrence counts, a restricted equation family or only compressed solution sizes do not settle the general claim. Proving membership of satisfiability in NP by an unrelated argument does not by itself establish this specific length bound.

context_blocks.text: Conjecture B concerns the length of a shortest solution. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 establish that this conjecture would imply the separate NP-membership conjecture for satisfiability. The implication depends on the proved compression property; an exponentially long explicit witness alone is not a polynomial-size certificate.

The source fixes letters and permits variable substitutions in the free monoid, hence allows erasing substitutions. The card retains its explicit occurrence-based equation size and uses a universal polynomial exponent to resolve the phrase singly exponential.

Jeż gives an independent proof of a doubly exponential general bound on the shortest common-word length. A bound of that scale does not establish the single-exponential claim, and bounds on repeated periodic blocks are not automatically bounds on the full solution length.

The 2026 paper gives stronger parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. It still describes membership in NP as open for unrestricted word equations. The fixed-variable, constant-free structural result does not cover the arbitrary equations in this card.

sentences: A word equation asks for consistent substitutions of finite strings that make two concatenations identical.
The conjecture says that every satisfiable equation of size n has some solution whose variable images have length at most two to a fixed polynomial in n.
The bound must hold uniformly over all finite alphabets and arbitrarily many variable occurrences, with empty substitutions allowed.
Known compression results make this length conjecture sufficient for NP membership of general word-equation satisfiability.
Doubly exponential bounds and newer results for restricted equation families do not meet the universal single-exponential target.
